A plywood plate must never go to the mill as a template: this folder is derived-never-authoritative, and a physical part is far more persuasive than a sheet.

## [machine/steel-prep.md](machine/steel-prep.md)  (18)

Cold-rolled sheet ships with a rust-preventive oil on it. Sand it first and the oil is driven into the surface, nothing bonds to it afterwards, and there is nothing to see — the plate looks the same as one that was done properly.
- FLAG: [L56](machine/steel-prep.md#2-take-the-surface-down) — *Steel prep: scale off, paint on / 2 — Take the surface down*<br>What the acid and the pad leave behind is the hard part, and neither will shift it. That is the 80 % bare face with dark grey islands in it, and more of either tool does not change it.
- FLAG: [L69](machine/steel-prep.md#2-take-the-surface-down) — *Steel prep: scale off, paint on / 2 — Take the surface down*<br>Use a ceramic or zirconia disc on steel, not wood abrasive. Ordinary aluminium oxide glazes almost at once at 60, which reads as the scale winning again.
- FLAG: [L72](machine/steel-prep.md#2-take-the-surface-down) — *Steel prep: scale off, paint on / 2 — Take the surface down*<br>🔴 Empty the dust extractor before sanding steel, or fit a fresh bag. Coarse grit in a geared mode throws hot particles, and hot steel into a bag holding fine wood dust is a vacuum fire. Steel dust is conductive and abrasive as well, so it is hard on the extractor either way.
- FLAG: [L76](machine/steel-prep.md#2-take-the-surface-down) — *Steel prep: scale off, paint on / 2 — Take the surface down*<br>Take the whole face to one grit, not just the patches. Spot-treating is what produces the patchwork. A face worked three different ways reads as three different surfaces under clear, and the sheen still changes under primer.
- FLAG: [L97](machine/steel-prep.md#the-stains-a-maroon-pad-will-not-take-out) — *2 — Take the surface down / The stains a maroon pad will no…*<br>Stop sanding a pitted stain. Reaching the bottom of the pit means taking all the metal around it down to that depth, which is real thickness off the panel for a mark that paint covers.
- FLAG: [L109](machine/steel-prep.md#the-stains-a-maroon-pad-will-not-take-out) — *2 — Take the surface down / The stains a maroon pad will no…*<br>Naval jelly comes off at 5 to 10 minutes, and 15 is the label maximum. Longer does not dissolve more — it just leaves a heavier, darker phosphate layer, which is invisible under primer and a visible patch under clear. If it has hardened on the surface, fresh jelly on top of the hard stuff softens it; do not dry-scrape it off a face you intend to show. Rinse with plenty of fresh water, and repeat the whole cycle rather than leaving one application on longer.
- FLAG: [L115](machine/steel-prep.md#the-stains-a-maroon-pad-will-not-take-out) — *2 — Take the surface down / The stains a maroon pad will no…*<br>Rinsed with water, it flash rusts in minutes — faster than before, because the surface has just been stripped chemically clean. Towel, heat gun until it is dry through and not just dry on top, and coat it the same session. Do not rinse a face you are not ready to coat.
- FLAG: [L119](machine/steel-prep.md#the-stains-a-maroon-pad-will-not-take-out) — *2 — Take the surface down / The stains a maroon pad will no…*<br>Gloves on anything bare, and that includes carrying a panel to the bench. A hand mark etches into clean steel and comes back as a cluster of finger-sized blotches the pad will not lift.
- FLAG: [L146](machine/steel-prep.md#3-deburr-while-it-is-still-bare) — *Steel prep: scale off, paint on / 3 — Deburr while it is st…*<br>Do it now. A hole opened out or an edge filed after the paint is on is bare steel in the one place that is hardest to reach again.
- FLAG: [L173](machine/steel-prep.md#5-prime-inside-the-hour) — *Steel prep: scale off, paint on / 5 — Prime inside the hour*<br>It is a tie coat, not a finish. Self-etch is thin and porous by design — it bites bare metal and gives the next layer something to hold. Dark grey looks finished enough to stop at, and on its own it is not the moisture barrier that is the whole job at these joints. Something goes over it, even cheap enamel on a face nobody sees.
- FLAG: [L178](machine/steel-prep.md#5-prime-inside-the-hour) — *Steel prep: scale off, paint on / 5 — Prime inside the hour*<br>Nothing gets sprayed in a room with the mining rigs running. They move enough air to lay dust into wet primer through the ten minutes it takes to flash, and an aerosol puts a solvent vapour cloud around energised electronics with fans in it. Spray elsewhere, or shut them down and ventilate first.
- FLAG: [L183](machine/steel-prep.md#5-prime-inside-the-hour) — *Steel prep: scale off, paint on / 5 — Prime inside the hour*<br>A sacrificial zinc-rich primer is the wrong choice at these joints. - FLAG: [L203](machine/steel-prep.md#6-two-finishes-and-no-bare-metal-left-anywhere) — *Steel prep: scale off, paint on / 6 — Two finishes, and no…*<br>Nothing goes under the clear that you are not keeping. Every stain, fingerprint and bit of flash rust left on a show face is sealed in and permanent, and there is no second attempt. Settle step 2 on those faces before the can is opened. This is the one place the stains stop being cosmetic.
- FLAG: [L208](machine/steel-prep.md#6-two-finishes-and-no-bare-metal-left-anywhere) — *Steel prep: scale off, paint on / 6 — Two finishes, and no…*<br>There is no primer under the clear, so the clear is the only thing holding. Bare steel is the weakest substrate a 2K urethane gets asked to grip — the sanding key is all it has, and a breach lets rust creep under the film where it cannot be reached. Which is the price of the raw look, and it is paid in keeping the surface clean before spraying rather than in anything added afterwards.
- FLAG: [L217](machine/steel-prep.md#6-two-finishes-and-no-bare-metal-left-anywhere) — *Steel prep: scale off, paint on / 6 — Two finishes, and no…*<br>2K hardener is isocyanate. It is a respiratory sensitiser, the kind of exposure that makes the next one worse rather than the kind you get used to. Cartridge respirator at the absolute minimum, strong ventilation, and nowhere near the mining rigs.
- FLAG: [L249](machine/steel-prep.md#where-the-coating-stops) — *Steel prep: scale off, paint on / Where the coating stops*<br>🔴 Never put a coating between a bearing block and its plate, or under the casting's foot. Those mounting faces are ground reference surfaces and the machine's geometry is set off them. A film creeps under bolt load, is never the same thickness twice, and tilts the block — trading a corrosion risk that is not there for a geometry error that cannot be found afterwards. The casting's foot is worse again: it is stepped, and whether the bar holds it off its bearing face is still open.
- FLAG: [L273](machine/steel-prep.md#one-that-belongs-at-assembly) — *Steel prep: scale off, paint on / One that belongs at assem…*<br>Paint creeps under sustained bolt load, so a painted joint loses bolt tension. ## [machine/three-point-mount.md](machine/three-point-mount.md)  (2)

- FLAG: [L42](machine/three-point-mount.md#stiffen-it-against-racking-which-is-not-what-it-looks-like) — *The three load-bearing points / Stiffen it against RACKING,…*<br>DO NOT REBUILD THE BASE IN THE LEFTOVER 25-SERIES EXTRUSION. Depth is cubed and timber buys it cheaply: a 2x6 is of order twice as stiff as a 2550, and a 4x4 about seven times a 2525 and better in buckling. Timber also damps, where aluminium rings. Extrusion's one real advantage over timber here is dimensional stability - and that is precisely what the three-point mount above already solves, which is why it is not a reason to spend the extrusion on the base. Spend it on the machine's own structure, where spans are short and the rails locate off it.

An accessible row is not sufficient, which was an error in an earlier version of this file. To tilt the plate the gap must open progressively from the hinge - a little at the third row, more at the second, most at the first. Every bolt above the hinge has to be free. A torqued bolt three rows up does not permit the tilt; it just bends the plate. Permanent access would therefore need 12 of the 16 reachable, not 4.

- FLAG: [L285](linear-encoder/design-can-position-feedback.md#superseded-proposal---a-printed-carrier-to-lift-the-tape-clear-of-the-bolt-heads) — *1.4 Physical layout / SUPERSEDED: PROPOSAL - a printed carr…*<br>Why the bond to the aluminium is the whole design, and why plastic was nearly wrong. §1.4's standing rule is bond the full length so the band is dragged by its substrate and the scale tracks the machine's real thermal growth — with an explicit "do not improve it into a one-end anchor later". That rule works because the substrate overwhelms the band: the 45 × 4 aluminium strip is of order 12,000 kN axially against a 15 × 4 printed carrier's ~180 kN. Aluminium commands the steel band. A printed strip commands nothing, and if it is left floating — located only by the bolt heads — then the tape's own steel band becomes the stiff member and the assembly reports steel's 11.7 µm/m/K while the machine moves on aluminium's 23.1. That is precisely the failure the full-length bond exists to prevent, arrived at from a different direction, and segmenting makes it worse rather than better.

The rule above says prefer down or inward; this is the note that it has not actually been applied to three of the four axes. Decide it before the tape is cut, because the tape is one-shot PSA and the bracket design follows from the face.

- FLAG: [L67](commissioning/masses.md#why-these-were-weighed) — *Measured masses / Why these were weighed*<br>Reflected inertia is why the gantry's mass nearly vanishes from the motor decision, and these are the numbers that showed it. Through a 5 mm lead, load mass reaches the motor shaft as mass x (lead / 2π)² - and ../machine/stepper-sizing.md works that to 6.3 x 10⁻⁷ kg·m² per kilogram, which puts the whole 58 kg below the screw's own inertia. So these masses settle the structural questions - what the risers carry, what the three-point mount carries, what has to be lifted - and are very nearly irrelevant to motor sizing. Reading them the other way round is the mistake they invite.
